To examine the associations of nasal microbiota with disease-modifying therapies (DMTs), lymphocyte subsets and olfactory function in multiple sclerosis (MS).

Thirty patients with MS and 30 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs) were enrolled. Patients were classified as DMT-treated (MS[DMT+]) or untreated (MS[DMT-]). Olfactory function was assessed using the University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT). Lymphocyte subsets were measured by flow cytometry, and nasal microbiota were analysed by 16S rRNA sequencing.

Olfactory function was lower in MS than in HCs, and better in MS(DMTs+) than in MS(DMTs−) ( p =0.016, 95% CI 0.5614 to 4.941). NK cell counts were lower in MS(DMTs+) than in MS(DMTs−) ( p =0.049, 95% CI -244.7 to -0.2109). And NK cell counts in MS(DMTs+) correlate with UPSIT ( r =-0.527, p =0.029). Compared with HCs, MS(DMTs−) showed higher Shannon diversity ( p =0.038), increased Proteobacteria ( p =0.004), reduced Moraxellaceae ( p =0.037) and Enterobacteriaceae ( p =0.033), and enriched branched-chain amino acid biosynthesis ( p =0.026). In MS(DMTs+), Campylobacter, Anaerococcus, Peptoniphilus, Prevotella , and Finegoldia were positively correlated with circulating NK cells (all p <0.05).

DMTs may improve olfactory function in MS, possibly through modulation of circulating NK cell-associated immune status and nasal microbiota, in addition to controlling disease-related inflammation.

Keywords: disease-modifying therapies (DMTs), lymphocyte subsets, multiple sclerosis, olfactory, university of pennsylvania smell identification test (UPSIT)

Proposed associations among olfactory function, DMT treatment, NK cells and nasal microbiota in multiple sclerosis. DMT treatment was associated with improved olfactory function and coordinated changes in peripheral immune status and the nasal microbiota. Arrows indicate associations rather than causality.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a central nervous system disorder driven by autoimmune mechanisms, in which inflammatory activity results in demyelination and subsequent axonal impairment ( 1 ). It is one of the most common causes of non-traumatic disability among individuals aged 18–40 years, affecting an estimated 2.8 million people worldwide ( 2 ). Immune imbalance is a major contributor to MS pathogenesis, characterized by dysregulated expansion and infiltration of T and B lymphocytes ( 3 ). Patients during the remission phase are generally managed with disease-modifying therapies (DMTs). DMTs modulate immune cell activity, suppress lymphocyte-mediated responses, reduce relapse rates, and slow short-term disability progression ( 4 ). Some DMTs may also contribute to improved neurological function in MS ( 5 ). However, whether they ameliorate olfactory dysfunction remains unclear.

Olfactory function refers to the ability of an organism to detect and identify odors through the olfactory system ( 6 ). Patients with MS may experience olfactory dysfunction of varying severity, and recent evidence suggests that approximately 27.2% have olfactory impairment ( 7 ). However, the mechanisms underlying olfactory dysfunction in MS remain unclear. Abnormalities may occur at multiple sites along the olfactory pathway, and both olfactory bulb atrophy and neuroinflammation have both been reported in patients with MS ( 8 ). The nasal cavity is the first site of entry for odorant molecules, and the local nasal microbiota plays an important role in the proper development of the olfactory epithelium ( 9 ). Previous studies have reported a reduced abundance of Corynebacterium in patients with postviral olfactory dysfunction, suggesting that nasal microbiota dysbiosis may be associated with impaired olfactory function ( 10 ). The nasal microbiota is closely linked to olfactory function, and whether olfactory dysfunction in MS is associated with alterations in the nasal microbiota remains to be elucidated.
